analysis.investment_thesis: Jana Small Finance Bank trades below book (P/B 0.95) with a 22% revenue CAGR, but the 21.85% promoter holding and declining net profit (INR 670 Cr → 501 Cr FY24→FY25 despite revenue growth) signal both governance risk and asset quality stress. For a disciplined value investor, this is not a business I can hold with conviction for a decade.
key_strengths: Revenue growing at 22.3% CAGR (FY22-25) with total assets doubling to INR 38,464 Cr — scale is being built.
Trading below book value at P/B 0.95 with forward P/E of 6.17, suggesting deep value optically.
Borrowings declining (INR 4,411 → 3,377 Cr) while cash swelled to INR 4,449 Cr — liability-side improving.
key_risks: Promoter holding of only 21.85% — far below my 55% minimum; skin-in-the-game is absent and governance risk is unacceptable.
Net profit fell from INR 670 Cr (FY24) to INR 501 Cr (FY25) despite 16% revenue growth — signals rising NPAs and credit stress in microfinance book.
Finance costs grew 20.1% CAGR — nearly matching revenue growth — compressing NIM and making profitability fragile in any credit cycle downturn.
red_flags: Promoter holding at 21.85% — deeply insufficient; no founder conviction visible.
Profit declined 25% YoY (FY24→FY25) while revenue grew — classic NPA buildup signature in small finance/MFI segment.
Operating CF swung wildly: +859 Cr → -1,137 Cr → +708 Cr → +4,073 Cr — unreliable earnings quality.
ROE of 12.18% is below my 15% floor — capital not being deployed efficiently.
MFI/underserved lending book carries concentrated credit risk; stress cycles are brutal for this segment.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Jana Small Finance Bank has built scale rapidly — assets grew from INR 20,189 Cr to INR 38,464 Cr in three years — and the revenue trajectory at 22.3% CAGR is impressive on the surface. However, the FY25 profit decline from INR 670 Cr to INR 501 Cr, despite double-digit revenue growth, tells the real story: credit quality is deteriorating in the microfinance book, a sector-wide problem in FY25. Finance costs at INR 2,317 Cr are consuming the bulk of revenue (INR 3,050 Cr), leaving almost no margin for error. The OCF pattern is erratic — one severely negative year (FY23: -1,137 Cr) followed by a sudden surge (FY25: +4,073 Cr, partly capital-raise driven) — not the steady, predictable cash generation I require.

The non-negotiable dealbreaker for me is the 21.85% promoter holding. I built DMart and held the majority of the business through every cycle — that alignment is everything. A bank where promoters own barely one-fifth of the business, with FIIs at just 4.31% and DIIs at 14.29%, tells me institutional confidence is limited and governance accountability is questionable. ROE at 12.18% is below my 15% minimum, and small finance banks — especially those with MFI heritage like Jana (formerly Janalakshmi Financial Services) — are prone to violent NPA cycles. This is not a business I can understand deeply enough, hold for 10-15 years, and sleep at night. Pass.
